summary: Defines an SMTP service extension that lets an interrupted mail transfer be restarted later without resending everything sent before the interruption. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: If your phone call drops while reading a long story, you can start again from where you stopped.

questions: how to resume an interrupted smtp transfer
how to resume interrupted smtp transfers
what offset does server return on reconnection
subtitle: Resume interrupted mail transfers without resending everything that arrived before the break.

tldr.problem: When SMTP transfers very large messages over unreliable connections, an interruption can force the entire message to be sent again from the start, wasting bandwidth and network resources.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1845 defines an SMTP service extension where the client assigns a unique transaction identifier (TRANSID) to each mail transfer. If the connection is interrupted, the client reconnects, repeats the MAIL command with the same TRANSID, and the server responds with an offset telling the client how many octets it successfully stored, so the client can resume from that point.
tldr.outcome: Clients no longer need to resend gigabytes of data from the beginning when a TCP connection drops mid-transfer. The server tracks partial state for at least 48 hours.

facts.label: Offset counting
facts.value: Starts at zero, counts octets in message data only (not envelope)

today: RFC 1845 remains an Experimental protocol from September 1995 and has not been updated or obsoleted. While the specification is sound, adoption of this extension for handling large mail transfers was limited. Modern approaches to interrupted transfers often use compression, chunked encoding, and improved connection quality rather than explicit checkpointing at the SMTP level.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
SMTP is the protocol for sending email across the Internet. It works well, but it was originally designed for small messages on reliable networks. When SMTP is used to transfer very large messages over less reliable connections, an interruption in the TCP connection can force the client to resend the entire message from the beginning.

RFC 1845 adds a checkpointing mechanism to SMTP. The client and server cooperate by assigning a unique identifier to each mail transaction. If the connection breaks during message transmission, the client can reconnect, give the same transaction identifier, and ask the server to tell it how much has already been stored. Then the client resumes sending from that point instead of starting over.
sections.eli5: When sending a huge email, if the connection drops, you can start again from where you stopped instead of sending everything again.

sections.title: The Extension Framework
sections.content:
The extension is named checkpointing. Servers that support it advertise the CHECKPOINT keyword in response to the EHLO command. The extension adds one optional parameter, TRANSID, to the MAIL FROM command.

The TRANSID value is a unique identifier structured as <local-part@domain>, similar to an RFC 822 message ID but designed to identify a specific SMTP transaction instance rather than the message itself. TRANSID values are case-sensitive and must not exceed 80 characters. The TRANSID is structured to ensure global uniqueness without a central registry: the domain should identify the SMTP client, and the local part should distinguish this transaction from other transactions from the same client.
sections.eli5: The mail system gets a new feature to bookmark where you are. You give the mail server a unique code that says this-is-my-copy-123@mycompany.com, and the server remembers it if something goes wrong.

sections.title: Checkpointing Service
sections.content:
When a client sends a MAIL command with a TRANSID parameter, the server stores the transaction identifier and retains the state and content of the transaction in non-volatile storage. The server keeps this information until the transaction is complete (when the client issues a QUIT command, starts a new transaction, or explicitly aborts).

If the connection is interrupted during DATA transfer, the server retains the state for a period of time defined by the server administrator, with a minimum recommended period of 48 hours. When the client reconnects and issues the same MAIL command with the same TRANSID, the server responds with status code 355 and an octet offset that indicates where the client should resume transmission. The offset is the count of message octets successfully received from the beginning, not including envelope data like MAIL FROM and RCPT TO commands.

The client then issues a DATA command and sends only the remaining octets starting from the offset. Once complete, the transaction finishes normally and the server deletes the saved state.
sections.eli5: The server remembers where it stopped taking your email. If you call back, it says I already have the first 50,000 characters; send the rest.

sections.title: State Preservation and Reconnection
sections.content:
The server preserves transaction state in non-volatile storage, meaning it survives server restarts and is intended to survive unexpected failures. When a client reconnects after an interruption, it must wait an appropriate period before retrying, as specified in RFC 1123 (Internet host requirements). The client should attempt to reconnect to the same IP address first (where the original transaction state is stored), but if that fails, it may try other servers listed for the mail exchanger.

If the client fails to restart the transaction on a different server, it is required to resend the entire message. RFC 1845 makes clear that waiting indefinitely for a server with interrupted state to come online is not acceptable; clients must eventually resend the message in full.
sections.eli5: The server writes down where it stopped so it remembers even if it crashes. You wait a bit before calling back, then try the same number first. If that fails, you have to start over with a different mail server.

sections.title: Usage Example
sections.content:
A typical flow begins when the client connects and sends EHLO to advertise its name. The server responds with its capabilities including the CHECKPOINT keyword. The client sends MAIL FROM with a TRANSID parameter. The client sends RCPT TO for each recipient, then DATA, and begins transmitting the message body.

If the connection breaks partway through the message (e.g., after 6135 octets have been successfully received), the server retains the state. After waiting an appropriate time, the client reconnects, sends EHLO, and issues the same MAIL command with the same TRANSID. The server responds with status code 355 and the offset 6135. The client then issues DATA again and sends only the remaining message octets starting from position 6135. Once the full message is transmitted, the server returns a normal 250 OK response and the transaction completes.
sections.eli5: First attempt: start sending email, connection drops after 6135 bytes. Second attempt: connect again, server says 355 6135 is where I stopped, send the rest, done.

sections.title: Status and Security
sections.content:
RFC 1845 is an Experimental protocol published in September 1995. It has not been updated or obsoleted. The RFC explicitly states that security issues are not discussed, as the extension is not believed to raise any security concerns beyond those already present in standard SMTP and email.

However, administrators should note that TRANSID values must be carefully constructed to ensure uniqueness, and the server must protect transaction state information in non-volatile storage. SMTP already requires authentication and encryption considerations in production environments; checkpointing should not weaken those protections.
sections.eli5: This is an experimental idea from 1995. Standard email security still applies; this just adds a bookmark feature.
